title: Open Economy Macroeconomics
description: Class 12 Economics: open economy and the balance of payments (current and capital account), the foreign exchange market and exchange-rate determination, and fixed, flexible and managed-floating systems.

topics.title: Open Economy and the Balance of Payments
topics.concept:
An open economy is one that trades with other countries — it has exports, imports and flows of money across its borders. (A closed economy, by contrast, has no foreign trade.) Almost every real economy, including India's, is open. To keep track of all its dealings with the rest of the world, a country prepares the Balance of Payments (BoP) — a systematic record of all economic transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world in a year.

The BoP has two main accounts:

  • The current account — records trade in goods and services and other current flows. It has two parts: merchandise trade (the export and import of goods, called visibles) and invisibles (services like software, tourism and shipping, plus income and transfers like remittances). The balance of just the goods part is the balance of trade (BoT).
  • The capital account — records flows of capital, i.e. borrowing, lending and investment between the country and the world (foreign investment, loans, banking capital).

So the current account is about income and spending with the world (mainly trade), while the capital account is about assets and liabilities (capital movements). A country is said to have a BoP surplus if its receipts from abroad exceed its payments, and a deficit if payments exceed receipts. The BoP gives a complete picture of a country's economic relationship with the rest of the world.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the balance of payments?
examples.solution:
A record of all foreign transactions.

  • A systematic record of all economic transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world in a year.
examples.answer: The BoP is a systematic record of all economic transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world during a year.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the difference between the current account and the capital account?
examples.solution:
Trade/income vs capital flows.

  • Current account: trade in goods and services and other current flows.
  • Capital account: flows of capital (investment, loans, borrowing).
examples.answer: The current account records trade in goods and services (and current transfers); the capital account records flows of capital (investment, loans, borrowing).

examples.problem: Example 3: Classify: (a) export of software services, (b) foreign investment in Indian shares.
examples.solution:
Service vs capital flow.

  • (a) Software services — an invisible in the current account.
  • (b) Foreign investment — a capital account item.
examples.answer: (a) Current account (invisibles — services); (b) Capital account (foreign investment).

recap:
• Open economy = trades with the world (vs closed economy).
  • Balance of Payments (BoP) = record of all foreign transactions in a year.
  • Current account: merchandise (visibles) + invisibles (services, income, transfers); goods balance = balance of trade. Capital account: investment, loans, borrowing.
  • BoP surplus (receipts > payments) / deficit (payments > receipts).

quiz.q: The balance of payments records transactions between a country and:
quiz.explanation: BoP records transactions with the rest of the world.

quiz.q: Foreign investment and loans are recorded in the:
quiz.explanation: Capital flows are recorded in the capital account.

topics.title: The Foreign Exchange Market and Exchange Rate
topics.concept:
To trade with other countries, we must exchange our currency for theirs. The foreign exchange market is where currencies are bought and sold, and the exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another — for example, ₹83 per US dollar. Like any price, in a free market the exchange rate is set by the demand for and supply of foreign exchange.

  • The demand for foreign exchange (e.g. dollars) comes from those who need foreign currency — importers (to buy foreign goods), people travelling or studying abroad, and investors sending money out. The demand curve slopes downward: when the foreign currency is cheaper (fewer rupees per dollar), people demand more of it.
  • The supply of foreign exchange comes from those who bring foreign currency in — exporters (paid in dollars), foreign tourists, and foreign investment and remittances. The supply curve slopes upward: when the foreign currency is dearer (more rupees per dollar), more is supplied.

The exchange rate settles where the two curves cross — the equilibrium exchange rate, where the demand for and supply of foreign exchange are equal:

examples.solution:
The price of one currency in another.

  • The price of one currency in terms of another (e.g. ₹83 per dollar).
examples.answer: The exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another (e.g. ₹83 = $1).

examples.problem: Example 2: Who demands and who supplies foreign exchange?
examples.solution:
Money going out vs coming in.

  • Demand: importers, travellers/students abroad, investors sending money out.
  • Supply: exporters, foreign tourists, foreign investment and remittances.
examples.answer: Demand comes from importers and those sending money abroad; supply comes from exporters and foreign money coming in.

examples.problem: Example 3: How is the equilibrium exchange rate determined in a free market?
examples.solution:
Demand meets supply.

  • Where the demand for and supply of foreign exchange are equal (the curves cross).
examples.answer: Where the demand for and supply of foreign exchange are equal — the intersection of the two curves.

recap:
• Foreign exchange market: where currencies are traded; exchange rate = price of one currency in another.
  • Demand for forex (importers, money sent out) slopes down; supply (exporters, money coming in) slopes up.
  • Equilibrium exchange rate = where demand for and supply of forex are equal.

options: Price of one currency in terms of another
quiz.explanation: The exchange rate is the price of one currency in another.

quiz.q: In a free market, the exchange rate is determined by the demand for and ____ of foreign exchange.
quiz.explanation: Like any price, it is set by demand and supply of foreign exchange.

topics.title: Exchange Rate Systems and Currency Changes
topics.concept:
Countries manage their exchange rates in different ways. The main exchange rate systems are:

  • Fixed exchange rate — the government/central bank fixes the rate and keeps it constant by buying or selling foreign exchange. It gives stability and certainty for trade, but the central bank must hold large reserves to defend the rate.
  • Flexible (floating) exchange rate — the rate is left to the free market, set by the demand for and supply of foreign exchange, and it changes from day to day. It needs no reserves to defend, but can be volatile.
  • Managed floating — a mixture used by most countries (including India): the rate floats freely most of the time, but the central bank intervenes (buys or sells forex) to smooth out big swings. This combines flexibility with some stability.

When the value of a currency changes, the words depend on the system:

  • Under a flexible system, a market fall in the rupee's value is depreciation (the rupee buys fewer dollars; it takes more rupees per dollar) and a rise is appreciation.
  • Under a fixed system, a deliberate official lowering of the currency's value is devaluation, and an official raising is revaluation.

The economic effect is the same in both cases: when the rupee weakens (depreciates/devalues), imports become costlier (so petrol and foreign goods cost more) but exports become cheaper and more competitive abroad; when the rupee strengthens, the opposite happens. So exchange rates connect the domestic economy to the world — completing our study of macroeconomics in an open economy.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the difference between a fixed and a flexible exchange rate?
examples.solution:
Government-set vs market-set.

  • Fixed: the rate is fixed by the government/central bank.
  • Flexible: the rate is set by market demand and supply and changes freely.
examples.answer: A fixed rate is set and held constant by the central bank; a flexible rate is set by market demand and supply and changes freely.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the difference between depreciation and devaluation?
examples.solution:
Market fall vs official lowering.

  • Depreciation: a fall in the currency's value in a flexible market.
  • Devaluation: a deliberate official lowering under a fixed system.
examples.answer: Depreciation is a market fall in a currency's value (flexible system); devaluation is a deliberate official lowering (fixed system).

examples.problem: Example 3: If the rupee depreciates against the dollar, what happens to imports and exports?
examples.solution:
A weaker rupee.

  • Imports become costlier (more rupees per dollar).
  • Exports become cheaper and more competitive abroad.
examples.answer: Imports become costlier and exports become cheaper (more competitive) when the rupee depreciates.

recap:
• Systems: fixed (central bank holds the rate; needs reserves), flexible (market-set; volatile), managed floating (float + intervention — India).
  • Depreciation/appreciation = market fall/rise (flexible); devaluation/revaluation = official lowering/raising (fixed).
  • A weaker rupee → imports costlier, exports cheaper; a stronger rupee → opposite.

quiz.q: An exchange rate set by market demand and supply is a:
quiz.explanation: A market-determined rate is a flexible (floating) exchange rate.

quiz.q: A deliberate official lowering of a currency's value under a fixed system is:
quiz.explanation: An official lowering under a fixed system is devaluation.

questions.q: An economy that trades with other countries is a/an:
questions.explanation: An economy with foreign trade is an open economy.

questions.q: A record of all economic transactions between a country and the rest of the world is the:
questions.explanation: That record is the balance of payments.

questions.q: The two main accounts of the BoP are the current account and the:
questions.explanation: The BoP has a current account and a capital account.

questions.q: Export and import of goods (visibles) are part of the:
questions.explanation: Merchandise trade (goods) is in the current account.

questions.q: Foreign investment and loans are recorded in the:
questions.explanation: Capital flows are in the capital account.

questions.q: The balance of just the goods part of the current account is the:
questions.explanation: The goods balance is the balance of trade.

questions.q: The market where currencies are bought and sold is the:
questions.explanation: Currencies are traded in the foreign exchange market.

questions.q: The exchange rate is the:
options: Price of one currency in terms of another
questions.explanation: The exchange rate is the price of one currency in another.

questions.q: The demand for foreign exchange comes mainly from:
options: Importers and those sending money abroad
questions.explanation: Importers and those sending money out demand foreign exchange.

questions.q: The supply of foreign exchange comes mainly from:
options: Exporters and foreign money coming in
questions.explanation: Exporters and inflows supply foreign exchange.

questions.q: An exchange rate fixed and held by the central bank is a:
questions.explanation: A central-bank-fixed rate is a fixed exchange rate.

questions.q: A market-determined exchange rate that changes freely is:
questions.explanation: A market-set, freely changing rate is flexible.

questions.q: The system India follows, combining a float with central-bank intervention, is:
questions.explanation: India uses a managed floating exchange rate.

questions.q: A market fall in the value of a currency (flexible system) is:
questions.explanation: A market fall is depreciation.

questions.q: When the rupee depreciates, imports become:
questions.explanation: A weaker rupee makes imports costlier (exports cheaper).

questions.q: Money sent home by Indians working in the Gulf (remittances) appears in India's BoP as:
options: A supply of foreign exchange (current-account invisible)
questions.explanation: Remittances bring foreign currency in, supplying forex and entering the current account as an invisible.

questions.q: If the demand for dollars rises (more imports) while supply is unchanged, the rupee will:
questions.explanation: Greater demand for dollars raises their rupee price, so the rupee weakens (depreciates).

questions.q: A weaker rupee helps Indian exporters because their goods become:
questions.explanation: Foreigners need fewer of their own dollars to buy rupee-priced goods, boosting export competitiveness.

questions.q: Under a managed float, the RBI sells dollars when the rupee falls too fast in order to:
options: Increase the supply of dollars and support the rupee
questions.explanation: Selling reserves adds to dollar supply, easing the rupee's slide — intervention within a float.

questions.q: Devaluation differs from depreciation mainly in that devaluation is:
options: A deliberate official act under a fixed-rate system
questions.explanation: Devaluation is a policy decision to lower a fixed rate, whereas depreciation is a market-driven fall.

questions.q: A persistent current-account deficit means a country's payments for imports and other current items exceed its:
options: Receipts from exports and other current inflows
questions.explanation: A current-account deficit arises when current outflows exceed current inflows (often financed by the capital account).

questions.q: A fixed exchange rate gives stability but requires the central bank to hold large:
options: Foreign exchange reserves to defend the rate
questions.explanation: To keep the rate fixed the central bank must buy/sell forex, which needs ample reserves.

questions.q: Foreign investment buying Indian company shares is recorded in the ____ and supplies foreign exchange.
questions.explanation: Inward investment is a capital-account flow that also brings in (supplies) foreign currency.

questions.q: A rising rupee (appreciation) tends to make a foreign holiday for an Indian tourist:
questions.explanation: A stronger rupee buys more foreign currency, so spending abroad becomes cheaper.

questions.q: Exchange rates are important in macroeconomics because they link the domestic economy to the:
options: Rest of the world (trade and capital flows)
questions.explanation: The exchange rate channels how foreign trade and capital flows affect domestic output and prices.
